items.title: How to Help Someone Change: The Samurai Guide to Giving Feedback
items.description: Few things in life are more exasperating than seeing the potential in someone you love and seeing them continually fall short of it, stumbling again and again over the same self-erected roadblocks of character and conduct, comporting themselves in a manner painfully inferior to what you know them to be capable of. items.title: How Not to Waste Your Life
items.description: “Let me not seem to have lived in vain,” the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe whispered on his deathbed, not realizing that the astronomical tables he was leaving behind would become the portal through which Kepler arrives at the laws of planetary motion; not realizing that the measure of an unwasted life is not what outlives it but how it was lived — how much integrity and authenticity and creative vitality filled these numbered days, these unrepeatable hours. items.title: Sleep and the Meaning of Life: Fernando Pessoa on the Existential Dimension of the Horizontal Hours
items.description: One of the most important things I have learned about living is that, in any life of purpose and creative vitality, you must be as religious and disciplined about your sleep as about your work. items.title: How to Love the World More: George Saunders on the Courage of Uncertainty
items.description: "In a world full of people who seem to know everything, passionately, based on little (often slanted) information, where certainty is often mistaken for power, what a relief it is to be in the company of someone confident enough to stay unsure (that is, perpetually curious)."

items.title: How to Love: Legendary Zen Buddhist Teacher Thich Nhat Hanh on Mastering the Art of “Interbeing”
items.description: "To love without knowing how to love wounds the person we love."

items.title: Carl Jung on Creativity
items.description: The question of what it takes to create — to make something of beauty and substance that touches other lives across space and time — is one of the deepest, oldest questions, perhaps because the answer to it is so unbearably simple: everything. We bring everything we are and everything we have lived to every smallest creative act — every experience, every dream, every memory, every unremembered impression, every unconsciously absorbed influence. items.title: Dostoyevsky in Love
items.description: “I love her happiness more than my own.”

items.title: How to Keep Life from Becoming a Parody of Itself: Simone de Beauvoir on the Art of Growing Older
items.description: "In old age we should wish still to have passions strong enough to prevent us turning in on ourselves."

items.title: G.K. Chesterton on the Dandelion and the Meaning of Life
items.description: Recovering the "forgotten blaze or burst of astonishment at our own existence" alive in the back of our modernity-deadened minds.

items.title: How to Bear Your Sorrows: Nick Cave on Integrating the Darkness of Loss with the Bright Ongoingness of Life
items.description: Few things in our culture are more wounding than the concept of healing — as if the pains and losses that we suffer are an illness, a malfunction of the psyche to be cut out like a tumor, rather than a natural function of being alive, of feeling life deeply and living it fully. items.title: Antidotes to Fear of Death: Astronomer and Poet Rebecca Elson’s Stunning Cosmic Salve for Existential Tremors
items.description: "Sometimes as an antidote to fear of death, I eat the stars."

items.title: Epictetus on Love and Loss: The Stoic Strategy for Surviving Heartbreak
items.description: "Who is good if he knows not who he is? and who knows what he is, if he forgets that things which have been made are perishable, and that it is not possible for one human being to be with another always?"

items.title: From Mitochondria to Minds: The Illustrated Science of the Psychedelic Dream Called Life
items.description: Like consciousness, like music, like love, life itself didn’t have to exist — nothing in the fundamental laws demands it. The universe could have gone on lapping at itself as a horizonless sea of pure spacetime, black and lifeless as the inside of a skull. But, in a whisper that soon became a symphony, life arose to give us such ceaseless wonders as the ghost pipe and the ginkgo, the bowerbird and the eye of the scallop. items.title: Albert Camus on the Three Antidotes to the Absurdity of Life
items.description: "In a world whose absurdity appears to be so impenetrable, we simply must reach a greater degree of understanding among men, a greater sincerity."

items.title: Notes on Complexity: A Buddhist Scientist on the Murmuration of Being
items.description: "You are this body, and you are these molecules, and you are these atoms, and you are these quantum entities, and you are the quantum foam, and you are the energetic field of space-time, and, ultimately, you are the fundamental awareness out of which all these emerge."
